reason: The sources provide multi-site verified facts detailing the discovery, ISS photography, geological origins, and lunar connections of Madagascar's Saririaky anorthosite massif.
story: When you look at the Moon on a clear night, the bright, reflective highlands visible to your naked eye are built almost entirely of anorthosite. Over four billion years ago, a global ocean of molten rock covered the young Moon. As it cooled, lightweight feldspar crystals floated to the top like froth, freezing into an ancient lunar crust. Apollo astronauts brought back precious fragments, but lunar samples remain exceedingly scarce. In August 2026, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station peered down at southern Madagascar and spotted something extraordinary: a glowing, 40-square-mile white disc blazing against the arid red landscape. It was the Saririaky massif, a 600-million-year-old deposit of terrestrial anorthosite. Trapped in a violent shear zone during the collision that assembled the supercontinent Gondwana, this massive rock formation survived extreme tectonic forces, leaving a piece of lunar-like geology stranded right here on Earth.
angle: Astronauts aboard the Space Station photographed a brilliant 40-square-mile white circle in southern Madagascar made of anorthosite—the exact same rock that floated atop a magma ocean 4 billion years ago to form the bright face of the Moon.

claims.claim: Anorthosite is an intrusive igneous rock that forms when molten material cools and solidifies underground, allowing large crystals to develop.
Anorthosite is primarily composed of pale plagioclase feldspar minerals.
Anorthosite makes up the Moon's bright, reflective highlands, which are visible from Earth without a telescope.
The Moon's anorthosite highlands are more than 4 billion years old.
Lunar anorthosites crystallized from a vast magma ocean covering the early Moon, where lightweight minerals floated to the surface to form an outer crust.
Apollo astronauts returned samples of lunar anorthosite to Earth.
Because the supply of returned lunar rock samples is limited, scientists study Earth-based anorthosites as analogues for the Moon.
Anorthosite deposits in Montana's Beartooth Mountains have a chemical composition that closely resembles lunar anorthosite.
Terrestrial deposits of anorthosite occur in regions including eastern Canada, Scandinavia, southern India, and Madagascar.
In southern Madagascar, an anorthosite formation known as the Saririaky massif forms a striking, roughly circular bright outcrop.
On August 28, 2026, an astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the Saririaky anorthosite massif.
The photograph (ISS075-E-85249) was taken by an Expedition 75 crew member using a Nikon Z9 digital camera with a 400 mm lens.
The exposed rock of the Saririaky massif covers approximately 100 square kilometers (40 square miles).
The Saririaky massif formed in the late Precambrian eon, at least 600 million years ago.
The Saririaky massif is located inside a ductile shear zone, where heat and pressure deformed surrounding rocks into north-south-trending linear patterns.
The geological deformation in southern Madagascar occurred during the continental collisions that formed the supercontinent Gondwana.
The assembly of Gondwana united continental fragments that now constitute parts of Africa, India, Madagascar, Australia, and Antarctica.
Scientists hypothesize that a second massif located about 60 kilometers (40 miles) north was once connected to Saririaky and separated by boudinage.

disputed: Whether the northern massif was originally part of the Saririaky massif and pulled apart via boudinage is a hypothesis rather than settled fact; scripts should attribute it as 'scientists suggest' or 'according to one hypothesis'.

The exact crystallization history and age relationships of lunar magma ocean cumulates (ferroan anorthosite vs. magnesium-suite rocks) remain actively debated due to impact mixing; scripts should describe the magma ocean model generally without asserting an uncontested age order for sub-types.

The genetic origin of Proterozoic anorthosites on Earth (whether derived from mantle basalts fractionating at the crust base or strictly lower-crustal melting) is disputed; scripts should state that their exact formation process on Earth remains an ongoing subject of debate.
